Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verses 2–4:

﴿The revelation of the Book﴾ was mentioned in az-Zumar. ﴿Except with truth﴾ was mentioned many times. ﴿And for a specified term﴾ means the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Show me what they have created﴾. ﴿Bring me a Book﴾: this is a challenge (ta'jiz), because they have no book that proves associating partners with God. Rather, all the books are explicit in affirming monotheism (tawhid), a proof for tawhid and a refutation of the polytheists. So the command carries the meaning of a challenge. ﴿A share in the heavens﴾, that is, a portion. ﴿Or a remnant of knowledge﴾, that is, a trace of ancient knowledge that supports what they claim. It has been said: it means knowledge that you extract (tuthirunahu), that is, you bring out. It has also been said: it refers to the isnad (chain of transmission). It has also been said: it refers to the line-drawing in the sand (al-khatt fi al-raml), which the Arabs used for divination (takahhun). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A prophet among the prophets used to draw lines in the sand; whoever's line agrees with his, that is it."

Translation:

﴿And who is more astray﴾ — the verse. Its meaning: there is no one more astray than one who calls upon a god that does not answer him, and these are the idols, for they neither hear nor understand. For this reason He described them as being heedless of their worshippers' supplication, because they do not hear it.

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿And when mankind are gathered, they will be enemies to them﴾ — rendered as the meaning, keeping markers.

Translation:

﴿And when mankind are gathered, they will be enemies to them﴾ — meaning: the idols will be enemies to those who worshipped them. ﴿And they will deny their worship﴾ — the pronoun in "they" refers to the idols: that is, the idols will disown those who worshipped them. The idols were mentioned with pronouns like those used for rational beings because what is attributed to them is what is attributed to rational beings: responding, heedlessness, and enmity.

Translation of the passage:

﴿Say: "If I have invented it, then you cannot avail me anything against Allah."﴾ That is: were I to invent it, Allah would punish me for the invention with a punishment that you could not repel, and you would not be able to possess anything to turn it away from me. So how could I invent it and expose myself to the punishment of Allah? ﴿He is most knowing of what you spread forth in it.﴾ That is, of what you say. It is said: "afada al-rajul fi al-hadith" (he plunged into the talk) when he dove into it and persisted in it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 9:

﴿Say: I am not an innovation among the messengers.﴾ Bid' and badi' (بدع والبديع) refer to things of which the like has never been seen. The meaning: I was not the first messenger, and I have not brought a matter that no one before me brought. Rather, I have brought what many people before me brought, so why do you deny that? ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you.﴾ On this there are four opinions. The first is that it concerns the matter of the Hereafter, and that this was before he knew that he would be in Paradise, and before he knew that the believers would be in Paradise and the disbelievers in the Fire. This is far-fetched, because he had known that from the very beginning of what God sent him with. The second is that it concerns the matter of this world: that is, I do not know what God will decree for me and for you, since the decrees of God are hidden. This is the most apparent opinion. The third: I do not know what will be done with me or with you in terms of commands and prohibitions and what the Shari'ah (sharia, the sacred law) requires. The fourth: that this was at the time of the Hijrah, when the Messenger of God ﷺ had seen in a dream that he would migrate to a land with palm trees, and the Muslims became anxious because of the delay in that, so this verse was revealed.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 10:

﴿Say: Have you considered? If it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it﴾. The meaning of the verse: Have you considered, if the Qur'an is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, are you not wrongdoers? Then the statement "are you not wrongdoers" was omitted, though it is the answer (jawab), because what follows indicates it: that Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its likeness﴾. This clause is joined (ma'tuf) to the clause before it, so the meaning is: Have you considered, if the fact that the Qur'an is from Allah combines with the testimony of a witness from the Children of Israel to its likeness, and then this witness believed in it while you disbelieved, are you not the most astray of people and the most wrongdoing of people?

Scholars differed about the witness mentioned, in three opinions. The first is that he is 'Abdullah ibn Salam. On this view, some said the verse is Madani, since he only embraced Islam in Madinah; others said it is Makki, and that he reported his testimony before it occurred, and then it happened as he had reported. 'Abdullah ibn Salam used to say: "The verse was revealed concerning me." The second is that he was a man from the Children of Israel who was in Makkah. The third is that he was Musa (peace be upon him), and al-Tabari preferred this view.

The pronoun in "its likeness" refers to the Qur'an, meaning he testifies to something like it in what it brought of tawhid, promise and warning. The pronoun in "believed" refers to the witness. If he is 'Abdullah ibn Salam or the other man, his belief is clear. If he is Musa (peace be upon him), his belief is his affirmation of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his giving good news of him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 11:

﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ That is: had Islam been good, these people would not have preceded us to it. The ones who uttered this statement were the notables of Quraysh when the weak ones embraced Islam, such as Bilal, Ammar and Suhayb. It has also been said that rather it was uttered by Kinana and tribes of the Arabs when Ghifar, Muzayna and Juhayna embraced Islam. And it has been said: rather, it was uttered by the Jews when Abdullah ibn Salam embraced Islam. The first view is more likely (arjah), because the verse is Meccan, and the statement of Quraysh was made in Mecca. As for the statement of the others, it was after the Hijra. The meaning of "those who believed" is "on account of those who believed": that is, they said this about them in their absence, and the meaning is not that they addressed them with these words, for had it been an address, they would have said, "You did not precede us."

﴿And since they have not been guided by it, they will say: "This is an ancient falsehood."﴾ That is: since they were not guided by it, they said, "This is an ancient falsehood." Similar to this is what came in the proverb: "Whoever is ignorant of something opposes it." He described it as ancient because it has been said in earlier times.

If it is asked: how can "fa-sa-yaqulun" (so they will say) govern "idh," which refers to the past, while the governing verb is in the future? The answer: the governing element of "idh" is omitted, its estimated meaning being, "when they were not guided by it, their obstinacy became evident, so they will say..." Al-Zamakhshari said this. It appears to me that "idh" here carries the sense of causation (ta'lil, giving a reason), not the temporal sense of the past, so the question does not arise. The meaning is that they said: "This is a falsehood," because they were not guided by it. "Idh" has come in the sense of causation in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, and among its examples is ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged [yourselves]﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 39], that is, because of your wrongdoing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verses 12–13:

﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and a mercy﴾. The pronoun in *qablihi* ("before it") refers to the Qur'an, and "the Book of Moses" is the Torah. *Imaman* (إِمَاماً) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a noun in the accusative that describes the state of another noun), and its meaning is: one follows it. ﴿And this is a Book confirming [it] in the Arabic tongue﴾. The demonstrative *hadha* ("this") refers to the Qur'an. The meaning of *muṣaddiq* ("confirming") is that it confirms what came before it of the Books, and we have mentioned this in Al-Baqarah [89]. *Lisanan* (لِّسَاناً) is a ḥāl from the pronoun in *muṣaddiq*. It was also said that it is a maf'ul bihi (direct object) of *muṣaddiq*, meaning: it confirmed the one who possesses an Arabic tongue, and this is Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this view. ﴿They stood firm﴾ (*istaqamu*, ٱسْتَقَامُواْ): this was mentioned in Ha Mim al-Sajdah [30].

﴿إِحْسَاناً﴾ (ihsanan, "kindness") is mentioned in Surah al-'Ankabut [29:8].

﴿حَمَلَتْهُ أُمُّهُ كُرْهاً وَوَضَعَتْهُ كُرْهاً﴾ ("His mother bore him with hardship, and gave birth to him with hardship"). That is, she carried him with difficulty and delivered him with difficulty. It is said that *kurhan* may be read with a fatha or a damma on the *kaf*, with the same meaning. ﴿وَحَمْلُهُ وَفِصَٰلُهُ ثَلٰثُونَ شَهْراً﴾ ("His carrying and his weaning are thirty months"). That is, the period of his carrying and his nursing is thirty months. This can only be true if one of the two periods is reduced. Either the gestation is six months and the nursing is two full years, or the gestation is nine months and the nursing is two years less three months. From this, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) and the scholars derived that the minimum period of gestation is six months. The period of nursing is expressed as *fisal* (weaning), which is the end of nursing. ﴿بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُ﴾ ("he reached his maturity") is mentioned in Surah Yusuf [12:22]. ﴿وَبَلَغَ أَرْبَعِينَ سَنَةً﴾ ("and reached forty years") is the limit of full intellect and strength. It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), and it is also said that it is general. ﴿فِيۤ أَصْحَابِ ٱلْجَنَّةِ﴾ ("among the companions of the Garden") means among the group of the companions of the Garden, just as you say: "I saw so-and-so among the people," meaning with the people.

And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!" [﴿وَٱلَّذِي قَالَ لِوَالِدَيْهِ أُفٍّ لَّكُمَآ﴾]. This verse applies in general to anyone who has this characteristic of disbelief and disobedience toward his parents. That it is general is shown by the Almighty's words, in the plural form, "Those are the ones upon whom the Word has been justified" [﴿أُوْلَـٰئِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ حَقَّ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقَوْلُ﴾]. Had He intended one specific person, He would have said, "That is the one upon whom the Word has been justified." The meaning of *uff* (أُفٍّ, an expression of annoyance) has already been explained in Surah al-Isra [23]. "Do you two promise me that I will be brought forth" [﴿أَتَعِدَانِنِيۤ أَنْ أُخْرَجَ﴾]: i.e., do you promise me that I will be brought out of the grave for resurrection? "And generations have passed before me" [﴿وَقَدْ خَلَتِ ٱلْقُرُونُ مِن قَبْلِي﴾]: i.e., generations of people have gone by, and none of them has been raised. "While the two of them call upon God for help" [﴿وَهُمَا يَسْتَغثِيَانِ ٱللَّهَ﴾]: the pronoun refers to his parents, i.e., they seek God's help against his denial, which they dislike in him. Then they say to him, "Woe to you!", and then they command him to believe. So he says, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients" [﴿مَا هَـٰذَآ إِلاَّ أَسَاطِيرُ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾]: i.e., the ancients have inscribed it in their books. That is a denial of the Resurrection and of the Sacred Law (al-shari'ah, the divine law).

For all there are degrees according to what they have done: that is, for the doers of good and the doers of evil there are degrees in the Hereafter according to their deeds. So the degrees of the people of Paradise ascend upward, and the degrees of the people of the Fire descend downward. "And that He may pay them in full" (liyuwaffiyahum) is a causal clause (ta'lil) connected to a verb that has been omitted, and it is attached to it; its estimated meaning is: He made their recompense degrees so that He might pay them in full their deeds. "And on the Day when those who disbelieve are exposed to the Fire" (wa-yawma yu'raḍu): the governing element of "the Day" is omitted, and its estimated meaning is: remember. "You squandered your good things" (adhhabtum ṭayyibatikum): its estimated meaning is that it will be said to them: "You squandered your good things." The "good things" (al-ṭayyibat) here means the pleasures of food and other things. Most of the readers recited adhhabtum with a single hamzah, as a statement (khabar), while Ibn 'Amir recited it with two hamzahs, as a rebuke (tawbikh). The verse concerns the disbelievers, as evidenced by His saying: "Those who disbelieve are exposed [to the Fire]." Yet it is, in addition to that, an admonition to the people of piety among the believers; for this reason 'Umar said to Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, when he saw him buying meat: "Do you not fear that you may be among the people of this verse?" "The punishment of humiliation" (al-'adhab al-hawn): that is, the punishment that is accompanied by humiliation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 21:

﴿And mention the brother of ʿĀd﴾, meaning Hūd, peace be upon him, ﴿when he warned his people in al-Aḥqāf﴾. Al-Aḥqāf is the plural of ḥaqf, which is a heap of sand. Scholars differed as to where it was located. It was said to be in Syria, and it was said to be between ʿUmān and Mahrah, and it was said to be between ʿUmān and Ḥaḍramawt. The sound view is that the lands of ʿĀd were in Yemen. ﴿And warners had already passed away before him and after him﴾, meaning they had come before him and after him. The word nudhur is the plural of nadhīr (warner). If it is asked: how can it be conceived that they came after him? The answer is that this sentence is an interjection (iʿtirāḍ), and it is a statement from God, exalted is He, that He had sent messengers before Hūd and after him. It was also said that the meaning of "those who came before him" refers to those who were before him in his own time.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 23:

﴿He said: "Knowledge is only with God"﴾. That is, say: "The punishment you have said, 'Bring it to us,' I have no knowledge of when it will occur; only God knows it. My duty is only to convey to you that with which I have been sent."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verses 24–25:

﴿When they saw it as a cloud advancing toward their valleys﴾. The ʿāriḍ (cloud) is the cloud that appears across the horizon of the sky. The pronoun in "raʾawhu" (when they saw it) refers either to what you threatened us with, or to the indefinite object of sight which is explained by His words ﴿ʿāriḍan﴾ (a cloud). Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is more eloquent and more correct in its grammatical analysis." It is narrated that they had suffered drought for a period, and when they saw this cloud they thought it was rain and rejoiced at it. Hūd (peace be upon him) said to them: "Rather, it is what you were hastening, a punishment." His words ﴿rīḥun﴾ (a wind) are either an apposition (badal) for ﴿mā istaʿjaltum﴾ (what you were hastening), or the predicate of an implied subject (khabar li-mubtadaʾ muḍmar). ﴿It destroys everything by the command of its Lord﴾: this is a general expression (ʿumūm) by which particularity (khuṣūṣ) is intended.

﴿وَلَقَدْ مَكَّنَاهُمْ فِيمَآ إِن مَّكَّنَّاكُمْ فِيهِ﴾ This is addressed to the Quraysh, in the manner of a threat. The meaning is: We established the 'Ad in that wherein We have not established you, in strength, wealth, and other things. Then We destroyed them when they disbelieved. Here *in* is negating, in the sense of *ma* (not). He turned away from *ma* out of dislike for combining it with the *ma* that precedes it (*ma* in *fima*). It was said that *in* is conditional, and its answer is omitted, its estimated meaning being: "If We had established you in it, you would have transgressed." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is excessive subtlety (*tanaṭṭu'*) in interpretation."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verses 27–28:

﴿And We had destroyed the towns around you﴾. He means the lands of 'Ad, Thamud, Saba' and others, and what is meant is the destruction of their inhabitants. ﴿Why did their gods not help them?﴾ The verse is in the form of a question, but its meaning is negation: their gods, whom they worshipped besides God, did not help them. ﴿As offerings (qurbanan)﴾, meaning they sought nearness to God through them, saying, "These are our intercessors with God." The accusative of qurbanan is in the sense of a circumstantial state (hal). It cannot be that qurbanan is a second object of "they took" (ittakhadhu), with "gods" (alihah) as a substitute for it, because this corrupts the meaning; this is what al-Zamakhshari said, though Ibn 'Atiyya permitted it. ﴿Rather, they strayed from them﴾, meaning they were lost to them and absent from their help when they were in need of them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verses 29–32:

﴿And when We turned towards you a company of the jinn﴾: that is, We inclined them towards it. The nafar (company) is fewer than ten. It is narrated that the jinn were seven, and they were all males, because nafar refers to men to the exclusion of women. They were from the people of Nasibin, and it is said from the people of al-Jazirah. There is a difference of opinion as to whether the Prophet ﷺ saw them. It is said that he did not see them and was not aware of their listening until Allah informed him of that. It is also said that he did know of them, prepared for them, and gathered with them. Various confused (mudtarib) reports on this have been transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud. The reason for the jinn's listening was that when they were barred from eavesdropping on the heaven by being pelted with meteors, they said: "This is nothing but because something has happened." So they roamed the earth looking to see what had caused this, until they heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting in the dawn prayer at the market of ʿUkaz. They listened to him and believed in him. ﴿Sent down after Musa﴾: this indicates that they were upon the religion of the Jews. It is said that they had not known of the sending of ʿIsa. ﴿Confirming what is before it﴾: mentioned in al-Baqarah [89]. ﴿The caller of Allah﴾: this is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ﴿He will forgive you of your sins﴾: "min" here indicates partiality (tab'id) according to the most correct view; that is, He will forgive you the sins you committed before Islam, while those after Islam are subject to Allah's will. It is said that the partial sense of "min" means that wrongful acts (mazalim) are not forgiven. It is also said that "min" is extra (za'idah). ﴿And will protect you from a painful punishment﴾: that is, from the Fire. People differ on whether the jinn have a reward beyond salvation from the Fire, or whether their only reward is salvation alone. ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse: it may be from the speech of the jinn, or from the speech of Allah the Exalted. The meaning of "not able to escape" (laysa bi-mu'jiz) is that he cannot escape.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 33:

﴿Do they not see﴾ — the verse is an argument for the resurrection of bodies from the creation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And He was not wearied by their creation﴾. It is said: "ʿayita bi-l-amr" (you were unable to know the matter) when you do not know it. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, knew how to create the heavens and the earth and perfected their creation, so there is no doubt that He is capable of giving life to the dead. ﴿Capable﴾ is in the place of nominative case because it is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). The preposition "bi-" entered because the negation at the beginning of the verse includes "inna" and its predicate. ﴿Yes indeed﴾ is the answer to what preceded, meaning: He is capable of giving life to the dead.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 46, verse 35:

﴿So be patient, as the resolute messengers were patient﴾ This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: be patient over the denial of your people. "The resolute ones" (Ulu al-'Azm) are Nuh, Ibrahim, Isa and Musa. It has also been said that they are the eighteen mentioned in Surat al-An'am, due to His saying: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It has also been said that they are everyone among his community who met hardship. And it has been said that all the messengers were "resolute ones," so "min" (from) in "min al-rusul" is for explaining the category (li-bayan al-jins) according to this view, while according to the previous opinions it is for partition (lil-tab'id). ﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾, meaning: do not seek to hasten the descent of the punishment upon them, for they are certainly going to it. When they are destroyed, it will be as if they had not remained in the world except for an hour of a day, because of how short their lives were. ﴿A proclamation﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated meaning being: "This with which you have been admonished is a proclamation," meaning: a sufficiency in admonition; or it is a proclamation from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, i.e., he has conveyed these admonitions and proofs.
